content: A malar rash, also known as a butterfly rash, is a distinct type of facial rash that serves as a clinical sign in certain medical conditions. It is frequently associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The term malar is derived from the Latin word for cheek. In lupus, the malar rash typically appears as a red or purplish discoloration on the face, often accompanied by mild scaling. Its characteristic shape resembles that of a butterfly, with the rash extending across the cheeks and involving the bridge of the nose. Epidemiology and Demographics The malar rash is observed in approximately 46-65% of individuals diagnosed with lupus. The prevalence of this rash can vary among different populations. Diagnosis Common Causes There are numerous other medical conditions that can produce rashes with a similar appearance to a malar rash. When lupus is suspected as the underlying cause, additional diagnostic steps are required. These typically include serological testing, such as an antinuclear antibody (ANA) test, and a thorough medical history to distinguish lupus from other potential conditions.
